title: TA9-03676
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant XXXXXXXXXX, is a citizen of Barbados and claims refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 ALLEGATIONS
The claimant fears persecution at the hands society in Barbados on account of his sexual orientation and the fact that he is HIV positive.
The Panel finds that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. ANALYSIS Identity
The claimant's identity is established through his oral testimony and the supporting documentation2 filed. Issues of Credibility and Subjective Fear

The claimant arrived in Canada on XXXXXXX, 2009. After investigation by Canadian Immigration Services, he was found with four fraudulent credit card numbers in his possession. He was asked by Immigration Services if he had used any of the fraudulent card numbers and he told them that he had used the American Express number to purchase his ticket to Canada.3

At the first seating of the hearing on December 14, 2010, the Panel asked the claimant why he had these fraudulent credit card numbers in his possession and he replied that, initially, he had intended to use one of the credit card numbers to purchase his travel ticket to Canada but a friend of his had ended up purchasing the ticket for him.

The Panel pointed out to the claimant that he had told Immigration Service that he had used one of the credit card numbers to purchase his ticket and asked him to explain the discrepancy. He replied that he was depressed when he had arrived in Canada.

I reject this explanation. I find it unreasonable that the claimant would acknowledge to Canadian Immigration Service that he had committed a fraud by using a fraudulent credit card number to purchase his travel ticket to Canada and run the risk of facing criminal proceedings if it had not been true. The claimant provided no reasonable explanation for this discrepancy and it undermines his credibility.

The claimant filed his Personal Information Form (PIF) and narrative4 on March 3, 2009. The original narrative is a single hand written page where the claimant states that he has HIV and that he cannot return to Barbados on account of his sexual orientation. The original narrative does not mention any incidents of threats, assaults, discrimination or persecution suffered by the claimant in Barbados on account of his sexual orientation.

The claimant filed an amendment to his narrative on June 16, 2010. The amended narrative is a typed seven page, single spaced document detailing a number of incidents in which the claimant suffered threats, assaults and persecution in Barbados.

In his amended narrative the claimant stated that, at the age of 17, he began a one and a half year homosexual relationship with a 29 year old man by the name of XXXXXXXXXX. The claimant stated that, in XXX of 2002, he spent a night at XXXXX house. XXXXX wanted to have sex with the claimant but the claimant refused because he had to work the next day. However, the claimant stated that XXXXX forced himself on the claimant and raped him.

The Panel asked the claimant why he had not mentioned this incident in his original narrative, and he replied that he was going through a lot of stress when he wrote his original narrative and he could not remember everything.

I reject this explanation. This is not a question of the claimant forgetting a minor detail of an event which he had written down in his narrative. This is a question of the claimant not mentioning in his original narrative that he had been raped by one of his former boyfriends. This is a major event in the claimant's story. He is basing his claim on his sexual orientation and it is reasonable to expect the claimant to have remembered when he wrote his original narrative that he had been raped by one of his former boyfriends. The claimant provided no reasonable explanation for this omission and it undermines his credibility.

The claimant stated that, after this incident, he sought the medical attention of a Dr. XXX. The Panel asked the claimant if he had a copy of Dr. XXX medical report and he stated that he had emailed a friend5 of his in Barbados, asking him to try and obtain a copy of the medical report from Dr. XXX. The Panel pointed out to the claimant that the copy of the email submitted to the Board does not ask the claimant's friend to obtain a copy of the medical report and asked the claimant to provide an explanation. The claimant remained silent.

It is reasonable to expect that the email which the claimant forwarded to his friend in Barbados for the purpose of obtaining Dr. XXX medical report would have this request in the body of the email. Such a request is not found in the email. The claimant provided no reasonable explanation for this omission and it further undermines his credibility.

In his amended narrative, the claimant stated that at the beginning of 2002, he began a homosexual relationship with XXXXXXXXX. He stated that after he moved in with XXXXX in XXXXXX of 2003, XXXXX became jealous of the claimant. In XXXXXX of 2003, XXXXX and the claimant became involved in an argument. XXXXX threw a pot of hot water on the claimant's face. XXXXX also threatened the claimant with a cutlass. The claimant managed to escape, went to the hospital and reported the incident to the police who offered the claimant no assistance.

The Panel asked the claimant why this incident had not been incorporated in his original narrative and he replied that he did not know that he had to write down everything. I reject this explanation. As with the incident with XXXXX, this is not a minor fact but a major event in the claim of the claimant. It is reasonable to expect the claimant to have remembered when writing his original narrative that he had been assaulted by XXXXX, that he had had hot water thrown to his face, that he had gone to the hospital to have injuries treated and that he had reported the incident to the police. The claimant provided no reasonable explanation for this omission and it further undermines his credibility.

In his amended narrative, the claimant stated that he obtained employment at the XXXXX XXXXXXXXXXX. He stated that when he went to visit his grandmother, he was verbally and physically assaulted by individuals on account of his sexual orientation. He stated that he was hit by rocks as he would walk to his grandmother's house.

The Panel asked the claimant why these incidents had not been included in his narrative, and he replied that he did not know what to put in. I reject this explanation. The basis of the claimant's claim is that he cannot live in Barbados on account of his sexual orientation. It is reasonable to expect him to remember these incidents when writing his original narrative for they would have demonstrated how he was treated in Barbados as a homosexual individual. The claimant provided no reasonable explanation for this omission and it further undermines his credibility.

The claimant stated in his amended narrative that in 2007 he travelled to New York City to meet XXXXXXXX, a gay individual whom the claimant had met through the internet. He remained in New York City for one year. The Panel asked him if he had applied for asylum during his stay in the United States of America (U.S.A.) and he replied that he had not for he did not know that he could apply. The Panel asked him if he had sought the assistance of a lawyer to determine whether he could apply for asylum and he stated that he did not.

I reject these explanations. The claimant bases his claim on his fear of returning to Barbados because he has suffered persecution in that country on account of his sexual orientation. He claims to be a practicing homosexual since 2002. Prior to his departure for the U.S.A., the claimant outlined a number of incidents where he was discriminated against in Barbados on account of his sexual orientation. In fact, in paragraph #30 of his amended narrative, the claimant states how life was better in New York in not having anyone calling him names and he was happier. It is reasonable to expect that when he arrives in the U.S.A. in 2007, he would make every effort to seek asylum. Not only did he not apply for asylum, he made no effort to seek legal advice to determine if he could apply.

The Panel finds this lack of effort to inquire about filing a claim in the U.S.A., a country which is signatory to the Convention, troubling and not demonstrative of the existence of his fear. As the Federal Court has stated: "... a refugee claim should not be looked at simply as one of many choices as to how best to seek status in Canada.6" It is a reasonable expectation that a person with genuine fear of persecution or harm in his home country will, absent a good reason, seek refugee protection immediately upon arrival in a safe country.7 The fact that he did not take this step soon upon arrival in the U.S.A. puts into question the genuineness of his fear. From the Panel's view, the apparent lack of urgency in his actions belies his claim of fear.

Professor Hathaway has said that it is appropriate to inquire into the circumstances of any protracted postponement of a refugee claim as a means of evaluating the sincerity of the claimant's need for protection.8

In the case at hand, the claimant exhibited a serious lack of urgency and inaction on making a claim in the U.S.A. and it demonstrates a lack of subjective fear should the claimant return to Barbados.

In 2007, the claimant stated that he came to Canada to get away from his lover in New York City. However, he was not allowed entry into Canada and returned to the United States where he was detained and deported back to Barbados.

The claimant stated that after returning to Barbados, he discovered that he was HIV positive.9 He was told by a friend of his that his lover in New York City would put wholes in the condom when they had sex. The Panel asked the claimant who it was that had told him that his lover had put wholes in the condom, and the claimant stated that he did not remember his name.

I reject this explanation. The claimant's amended narrative is a seven page typed single spaced document that is detailed as to names and dates that go back to the year 2000. He has a good memory for places, incidents and names that stretch well over 10 years, and yet he cannot remember the name of the individual who informed him of how he had been infected with HIV. I find it implausible that the claimant would not remember the name of the individual who told him that the claimant's lover in New York City had put wholes in his condom whenever they had sex. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant did not contract HIV from his lover in New York City.

On a balance of probabilities, I find that the events narrated by the principal claimant in his oral testimony and in his amended narrative did not occur. The Board has been upheld when rejecting major evidence which has been omitted from the PIF.10

Given the serious inconsistencies, discrepancies, omissions with respect to numerous major issues in this claim, I find that the claimant was generally lacking in credibility. I simply do not find that, on a balance of probabilities, any of the significant events that the claimant alleges happened to him, actually happened.

I find that the testimony of the claimant to be without credibility with regard to the material aspects of his claim. The major discrepancies and omissions within the story are fatal to his claim and give the claimant no credibility. I determine that he has not satisfied the burden of establishing that it is more likely than not11 that he would face a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture, if he were to return to Barbados.

I am obligated to make a determination on the evidence deemed credible and trustworthy. I find none. It is my determination that the claimant has not established a subjective or an objective basis to his fear, nor has he established any other element of the material aspects of his claim.
The claimant submitted a psychological report.12 However, the report is based on a story which the Panel does not believe. Therefore, I give the psychological report no weight.

Accordingly, the Refugee Protection Division finds, pursuant to section 107(2) of the IRPA, that there is no credible basis for his claim.
